value.overview: The Black-collared Hawk (Busarellus nigricollis) is a broad-winged raptor strongly associated with wetlands and shallow water. It is named for the dark crescent across the upper breast, below a pale buff-white head. Most of its range lies from southern Mexico through Central America and across tropical South America east of the Andes. It usually hunts from perches near marshes, ponds, slow rivers, flooded fields, and forest edges.
value.classification: The Black-collared Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. It is the only species in the genus Busarellus.
value.identification: Adults are medium-sized hawks with broad wings, a short tail, and mainly cinnamon-rufous underparts. The head is pale buff or whitish, often with fine dark streaking, and a conspicuous black crescent forms a collar across the upper breast. The flight feathers are mostly black, while the tail is brown with dark bands. Immatures are browner and more heavily streaked, with less sharply defined adult markings.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of tropical South America east of the Andes, reaching southern Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, and northern Argentina. In Costa Rica it is a scarce, local resident rather than a widespread common hawk. Reliable records are concentrated around wetlands and lowland waterways, including Río Frío and Caño Negro, with additional occurrences near Tortuguero, the lower Tempisque and Bebedero basins, and parts of the Osa Peninsula. It uses shallow marshes, lagoons, slow rivers, flooded fields, riparian woodland, and open lowland habitats with trees for perching.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident and not considered a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it is regarded as a local resident, although individuals may make short-distance movements in response to water levels and prey availability.
value.breeding: Black-collared Hawks build a large stick nest, usually in a tall tree near water, sometimes in an isolated or emergent tree above wetland vegetation. The nest is lined with smaller twigs and fresh leaves. Clutch size is commonly one or two eggs, though details vary across the range. Both adults participate in territorial activity and care for the young. A nesting record from Costa Rica confirms that the species breeds there, although breeding information for the country remains limited.
value.dietFeeding: Fish make up most of the diet. The hawk usually watches from a low or moderate perch and drops or plunges into shallow water to seize fish with its long, strongly curved talons. Specialized roughened surfaces on the feet may help it hold slippery prey. It also takes aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, crustaceans, and other small animals when available. Hunting is closely tied to calm, shallow water and exposed wetland margins.
value.behavior: This hawk often sits quietly on branches overlooking water, marsh edges, or flooded vegetation. It may make short flights between perches while searching for prey and can hover or plunge briefly when attacking fish. Pairs may perform high aerial displays involving circling, calling, dipping, and diving. It is usually solitary or seen in pairs, and its distribution is strongly patchy because suitable wetlands are unevenly distributed across the landscape.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered decreasing, but the species remains widespread and is not currently close to the thresholds for a threatened category.
